title: Symbol_level
summary:
The symbol level is a concept in knowledge-based systems coined by Allen Newell in 1982. In knowledge-based systems, agents choose actions based on the principle of rationality to move closer to a desired goal. The agent is able to make decisions based on knowledge it has about the world (the knowledge level). But for the agent to actually change its state, it must use whatever means it has available. This level of description for the agents behavior is the symbol level.

The symbol level distinguishes the implementation mechanisms (algorithms, data structures, code) from the knowledge level (the abstract information and goals an agent reasons about). It describes how an agent carries out its actions, as opposed to what it knows or why it acts. Whereas the knowledge level is world oriented, concerning the environment in which the agent operates, the symbol level is system oriented, including the mechanisms the agent has available to operate.

For example, in a computer program, the knowledge level consists of the information contained in its data structures that it uses to perform certain actions. The symbol level consists of the programs algorithms, the data structures themselves, and so on. The knowledge level rationalizes the agents behavior, while the symbol level mechanizes the agents behavior.
